title: Generosity
hookLine: an open heart and an open hand

cards: The craftsmen building the Tabernacle put down their tools and go to Moses with a problem. It isn't a shortage. It's the opposite.

Morning after morning, the people keep bringing gifts: gold and silver, blue and purple yarn, wood, skins, spun goats' hair. There is more than the work needs. So Moses sends word through the camp: no one bring any more.
And Exodus adds: "So the people were restrained from bringing." An appeal, called off because it worked.

teach.h: WHOSOEVER IS OF A WILLING HEART.
teach.b: Nedivut. Generosity: an open heart and an open hand. Turn it four ways.
First, the heart comes first. The call in Exodus went out to "whosoever is of a willing heart." Not to the richest, or to those who owed the most.
The gifts are called nedavah, a freewill offering: given because a heart moved, not because a bill came due. Second, the hand follows.
Deuteronomy, speaking of a neighbor in need, says not to harden the heart or shut the hand, but to open the hand to the poor. A soft heart with a closed hand is only a feeling.
An open hand with a hard heart is only a transaction.
Third, the trait under the duty. Jewish law treats tzedakah, which this path met long ago, as an obligation: owed to those in need whether you feel like it or not.
Some Mussar teachers describe nedivut as the trait underneath, the inner readiness that makes giving glad instead of grudging. The law says what to give. The trait shapes how it leaves your hand.
Fourth, it isn't only money. Exodus tells of women who spun yarn with their own hands and brought what they had spun.
Gold sat next to goats' hair in that collection.
Time, attention, a meal, a skill, a word of praise you could have kept: all of it can be brought. And it follows yesterday's zeal: the people didn't wait to be asked twice.

how: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box and drop coins in before Shabbat, and Mussar students work on nedivut by noticing whether their giving comes gladly or grudgingly.

games.q: you're Moses. the people have brought more gifts than the work needs, and they keep coming. what do you do?
o: send word through the camp: bring no more.
give the extra back to the richest families.
games.why: Moses sends word through the camp, and "the people were restrained from bringing."

practice: Turn your hands palm up and leave them open. Ask what you have that someone could use, not only money: an hour, a ride, a book you've finished, praise you've been holding back, and let one gift and one person come to mind together.
Check the heart: if it isn't given gladly yet, make it smaller until it is; if you pray, hold that person in your prayer as you decide.

wordCard.voice: Nedivut. Generosity: the willing heart behind the freewill gift, and the open hand that follows it. Today's word.
